definition: Nolot is a chess test suite with 11 positions from real games.
details: They were compiled by Pierre Nolot (French: [nɔ.lo]) for the French chess magazine Gambisco and posted on the rec.games.chess Usenet group in 1994. They were designed to be particularly hard for chess engines to solve at the time, although modern engines can find a solution near-instantaneously.

explainer.lead: Nolot is a chess test suite of 11 positions taken from real games, compiled by Pierre Nolot for the French chess magazine Gambisco and posted to the rec.games.chess Usenet group in 1994. It matters as a historical benchmark: it was designed to be especially hard for the chess engines of its time.

tiers.eli5: It is a short set of chess puzzles meant to stump the computer programs of the 1990s, like a puzzle book that was deliberately too clever for old chess robots.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it as a small sanity check on tactical strength alongside larger suites. Pitfall: modern engines solve it near-instantaneously, so it no longer discriminates between them and should not be treated as a meaningful ranking.
tiers.paperLevel: It is a fixed suite of 11 positions with a defined task of finding the correct continuation, not a statistical benchmark. Known limits: tiny sample, no standardization of time controls, and saturation by current engines.

explainer.example: Running an engine on the suite and seeing it return the right move for all 11 positions in fractions of a second shows the positions are no longer a challenge.
